evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 要 entry: Shuowen account, pronunciations, and cited usages
evidence.text: The entry reports the Shuowen explanation of 要 as “the middle of the body,” depicting a person holding the waist and analyzing it as 从臼 with 交省聲. It gives modern Mandarin yāo for the waist sense and yào for other senses. It cites 墨子·兼愛中 “昔者，楚靈王好士細要” for the waist sense; it also lists distinct uses glossed as pact, seek, invite, coerce and intercept, among others. Its listed examples show use categories, but do not by themselves establish a chronological semantic pathway.
evidence.title: [A03763] 要 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: 常用漢字二百字探源（金真姬）
evidence.field: 要 entry, forms and component analyses (PDF pp. 172–173)
evidence.text: The study lists a Shang oracle-bone example 合集8175, Western Zhou bronze examples 是要簋 and 伯要敦, followed by Spring and Autumn, Warring States, Qin and Han forms. It describes the oracle graph as 女, two hands, and a 日-like upper form, but records disagreement over the parsing: Li Xiaoding rejects 交省 as phonetic and interprets the shape as a woman holding her waist; another proposal treats it as a composite involving 臼, 女 and hands. The author identifies 要 as the original graph for 腰, with 肉 added later to distinguish the body-part word. These are reported scholarly analyses, not direct visual inspection of inscription artifacts.
evidence.title: 常用漢字二百字探源

evidence.source: 常用漢字二百字探源（金真姬）
evidence.text: The study cites 墨子·兼愛中 “昔者楚靈王好士細要,” 楚辭·離騷 “戶服艾以盈要兮,” and 荀子·禮論 “量要而帶之” as transmitted-text examples of 要 meaning waist. It reports later commentators explicitly equating 要 and 腰. These examples attest the waist sense in transmitted pre-imperial works, but the material inspected does not establish the earliest dated occurrence or a date for the proposed borrowing of other senses.

evidence.text: The dictionary separates readings and senses: yāo is listed with the waist sense and cited Mozi example, while yào includes key/essential, important, want/need, must, and imminent meanings. The entry cites examples from different transmitted works and later literature but does not date the development of these senses. Its distinction cautions against deriving semantic chronology from a modern list of glosses.

evidence.text: The study presents inscriptional forms separately from the transmitted textual waist examples. Its listed Shang and Western Zhou graph examples support an early graphic record for 要, while the inspected text does not show what word those particular inscriptional tokens record. The waist-word evidence it supplies comes from transmitted literature, and it does not provide an independently dated early inscription for the want/need meaning.

gaps: The cited primary 2010 article by 郭永秉 was not accessed; competing structural interpretations are supported here by the scholarly study's references to Li Xiaoding and Lu Shixian and by secondary reporting, not by inspection of that article.

The upper and hand-like elements of early 要 are disputed. The sources support reporting proposed analyses but do not establish an uncontested component-by-component interpretation. No component can confidently be classified as a phonetic element on the evidence inspected; the Shuowen 交省聲 explanation is an ancient dictionary analysis, not verified historical sound evidence.

The sources inspected do not date the first waist-word occurrence, establish which senses in the modern dictionary list came first, or demonstrate a dated borrowing event from a waist word into want/need or other meanings. A waist-to-pivot-to-essential pathway remains an unverified semantic proposal.

Although the scholarly study lists Shang and Western Zhou graphic exemplars, this research did not inspect their source artifacts directly. The study's inscription list does not establish the lexical reading of each particular token.

The official Unicode codepoint records for 要, 女 and 腰 returned internal errors. The harness-provided local readings were checked for notation and provenance but are not cited as externally verified readings.

The seal-script image is an identified, reusable modern vector redraw. No exact, inspected direct-image page for a usable inscriptional glyph was established in this run; Commons' linked Shang and Zhou alternatives led to category pages rather than a verified 要 file.
